A.line: Same question, opposite answers. Confucius urged the slow student forward and kept the eager one back.
A.exact: Tsze-lu asked whether he should immediately carry into practice what he heard. The Master said, 'There are your father and elder brothers to be consulted; why should you act on that principle of immediately carrying into practice what you hear?' Zan Yu asked the same, whether he should immediately carry into practice what he heard, and the Master answered, 'Immediately carry into practice what you hear.' ... The Master said, 'Ch'iu is retiring and slow; therefore, I urged him forward. Yu has more than his own share of energy; therefore I kept him back.'
A.source: Confucian Analects, Book XI, ch. XXI in Legge's numbering (11.22 in modern numbering), tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed. rev. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1893). Checked in the 1893 scan and on Wikisource.

A.line: Sometimes the best horse may be the worst horse, and the worst horse can be the best one.
A.credit: Shunryu Suzuki · Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (1970)
A.exact: Those who can sit perfectly physically usually take more time to obtain the true way of Zen, the actual feeling of Zen, the marrow of Zen. But those who find great difficulties in practicing Zen will find more meaning in it. So I think that sometimes the best horse may be the worst horse, and the worst horse can be the best one.
A.source: Shunryu Suzuki, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (New York: Weatherhill, 1970), Part One 'Right Practice', chapter 'The Marrow of Zen', pp. 37-38.

A.line: Tsiolkovsky, nearly deaf from a childhood fever, left school and taught himself. Today he is called the father of astronautics.
A.credit: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky · Space Hall of Fame, 1976
A.exact: As a boy, scarlet fever left Tsiolkovsky with permanently impaired hearing (Dictionary of Scientific Biography: 'almost completely deaf'). Unable to continue in school, he studied on his own from his father's books, and from 1873 to 1876 in the main Moscow libraries. In 1879 he passed the teaching examination without attending lectures, and taught at the Borovsk district school from 1880 to 1892. The New Mexico Museum of Space History calls him the 'Father of Astronautics and Rocket Dynamics'.
A.source: New Mexico Museum of Space History, International Space Hall of Fame inductee page (inducted 1976); Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography and Gale Encyclopedia of World Biography (Encyclopedia.com). Two sources agree; no age given because they differ (9 or 10).

A.line: The Buddha saw people like lotuses: some flourish under the water, some stand level, some rise above it.
A.credit: The Buddha, Samyutta Nikaya 6.1 · tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu (adapted)
A.exact: he saw beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much, those with keen faculties and those with dull, those with good attributes and those with bad, those easy to teach and those hard ... Just as in a pond of blue or red or white lotuses, some lotuses ... might flourish while immersed in the water, without rising up from the water; some might stand at an even level with the water; while some might rise up from the water and stand without being smeared by the water ...
A.source: Samyutta Nikaya 6.1, Ayacana Sutta ('The Request'), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu (1997), Access to Insight (CC BY-NC 4.0). Three lotuses only, as in the sutta.

A.line: Feynman counted by talking to himself. John Tukey counted by picturing numbers. Same task, different minds.
A.credit: Richard Feynman · What Do You Care…, 1988
A.exact: By that experience Tukey and I discovered that what goes on in different people's heads when they think they're doing the same thing ... is different for different people. ... It's natural to explain an idea in terms of what you already have in your head. (Story in the same essay: Feynman counted by 'talking' to himself, so he could read while counting but not speak; Tukey was 'visualizing a tape with numbers on it going by', so he could talk while counting but not read.)
A.source: Richard P. Feynman, as told to Ralph Leighton, 'It's as Simple as One, Two, Three', in What Do You Care What Other People Think? (New York: W.W. Norton, 1988); reprinted in Caltech Engineering & Science, Fall 1988, pp. 11-16.

A.line: Not too gentle, not too hard: you can get it in your hand and feel it in your mind.
A.credit: Zhuangzi, ch. 13, the wheelwright · tr. Burton Watson
A.exact: When I chisel a wheel, if the blows of the mallet are too gentle, the chisel will slide and won't take hold. But if they're too hard, it will bite and won't budge. Not too gentle, not too hard: you can get it in your hand and feel it in your mind. You can't put it into words, and yet there's a knack to it somehow. I can't teach it to my son, and he can't learn it from me.
A.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 13 'The Way of Heaven', tr. Burton Watson, The Complete Works of Zhuangzi (New York: Columbia University Press, 2013), revised wording. Under copyright: keep the quote to a line or two. Only the punctuation after 'not too hard' is changed (a dash in the book).

A.line: The world is going to need all of the different kinds of minds to work together.
A.exact: Now, the thing is, the world is going to need all of the different kinds of minds to work together.
A.source: Temple Grandin, "The world needs all kinds of minds", TED2010, February 2010 (transcript on ted.com)

A.line: If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer.
A.exact: If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away. It is not important that he should mature as soon as an apple-tree or an oak.
A.source: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), final chapter 'Conclusion'. Project Gutenberg eBook #205. Public domain.

A.line: The essence of my father's teachings: the yoga practice must be tailored to fit each person.
A.credit: T.K.V. Desikachar on T. Krishnamacharya · The Heart of Yoga, 1995 (adapted)
A.exact: The essence of my father's teachings is this: it is not that the person needs to accommodate him- or herself to yoga, but rather the yoga practice must be tailored to fit each person. [Also: My father's teaching first and foremost was based on the truth that each student must be taught according to his or her individual capacity at any given time.]
A.source: T.K.V. Desikachar, The Heart of Yoga: Developing a Personal Practice (Rochester, VT: Inner Traditions, 1995). Second line: T.K.V. Desikachar with R.H. Cravens, Health, Healing and Beyond (New York: Aperture, 1998).

A.line: What the child can do in cooperation today he can do alone tomorrow.
A.credit: Lev Vygotsky, Thought and Language, ch. 6 · tr. Hanfmann and Vakar
A.exact: What the child can do in cooperation today he can do alone tomorrow. [Russian original: «...то, что ребенок умеет делать сегодня в сотрудничестве, он сумеет сделать завтра самостоятельно.»]
A.source: L.S. Vygotsky, Thought and Language, ch. 6, tr. Eugenia Hanfmann and Gertrude Vakar (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1962), p. 104. Russian: «Мышление и речь» (1934), гл. 6; Собрание сочинений, т. 2 (Москва: Педагогика, 1982).

B.line: Momofuku Ando lost almost everything in 1957. In 1958, at 48, he launched the world's first instant noodles.
B.exact: In 1957 a credit union where Ando was a director went bankrupt, and he lost all his property except a rented house in Ikeda City, Osaka. In a shed he built in the backyard of his home, he worked on the product. Chicken Ramen, the world's first instant noodles, launched on 25 August 1958, when he was 48. Nissin: 'Ando, who realized a dream of many years at the age of 95, said, "There's no such thing as too late in life."' [Japanese: 人生に遅すぎるということはない]
B.source: Nissin Foods Group, 'Our Founder' (official page), and Nippon.com, 'Andō Momofuku: An Inventor Who Used His Noodle to Change Global Food Culture' (17 Apr 2018). Both agree on the story facts. No birthplace, no later legal history.

B.line: If another man succeed by one effort, he will use a hundred efforts... though weak, he will surely become strong.
B.credit: Doctrine of the Mean 20 · tr. James Legge (adapted)
B.exact: If another man succeed by one effort, he will use a hundred efforts. If another man succeed by ten efforts, he will use a thousand. Let a man proceed in this way, and, though dull, he will surely become intelligent; though weak, he will surely become strong. [Chinese: 人一能之己百之，人十能之己千之。果能此道矣，雖愚必明，雖柔必強。]
B.source: The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), ch. 20, closing lines, tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1. Checked on Wikisource, English and Chinese.

B.line: Ramanujan failed every exam subject except maths and became a clerk. In 1914 he went to Cambridge.
B.credit: Srinivasa Ramanujan, mathematician · MacTutor, St Andrews
B.exact: In Madras (1906) he passed mathematics but failed the other subjects of the First Arts exam. His 1912 application to be a clerk at the Madras Port Trust: 'I have passed the Matriculation Examination and studied up to the F.A. but was prevented from pursuing my studies further owing to several untoward circumstances. I have, however, been devoting all my time to Mathematics and developing the subject.' He began there on 1 March 1912, wrote to G. H. Hardy in January 1913, and went to Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1914.
B.source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Srinivasa Ramanujan' (O'Connor and Robertson, University of St Andrews), and English Wikipedia, 'Srinivasa Ramanujan' (application letter dated 9 Feb 1912). Two sources agree.

B.line: Slowly, slowly, you get a fine machete.
B.credit: Thai proverb · ช้า ๆ ได้พร้าเล่มงาม
B.exact: ช้า ๆ ได้พร้าเล่มงาม (cháa cháa dâi práa lêm ngaam). Variant: ช้า ๆ ได้พร้าสองเล่มงาม. TruePlookpanya: ค่อย ๆ คิด ค่อย ๆ ทำแล้วจะสำเร็จผล (think step by step, act step by step, and you succeed).
B.source: TruePlookpanya, 'สำนวนไทย คำพังเพย สุภาษิต' and 'สำนวนไทยหมวด ช., ซ.'; Thailand Starter Kit, '50 Useful Thai Proverbs and Idioms' (no. 8). English is our own translation.

B.line: Krylov wrote plays first. At 40 he published his first book of fables, and wrote about 200 in all.
B.exact: Krylov's first collection of fables, 23 in number, appeared in 1809 and met with such an enthusiastic reception that thereafter he abandoned drama for fable-writing ... some 200. ... he only discovered his true genre at the age of 40. [Russian Wikipedia: В 1809 году Крылов выпустил первое отдельное издание своих басен... 23 произведения]
B.source: English Wikipedia, 'Ivan Krylov'; Russian Wikipedia, 'Крылов, Иван Андреевич'; 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kriloff, Ivan Andreevich' (Wikisource). Three sources agree on 1809, 23 fables and the move from plays to fables.

B.line: The success of Yogis differs according as the means they adopt are mild, medium, or intense.
B.credit: Patanjali, Yoga Sutra 1.22 · tr. Swami Vivekananda
B.exact: 21. Success is speedy for the extremely energetic. 22. The success of Yogis differs according as the means they adopt are mild, medium, or intense. [Sanskrit 1.22: mṛdu-madhya-adhimātratvāt tato 'pi viśeṣaḥ] [Also 1.14: It becomes firmly grounded by long constant efforts with great love (for the end to be attained).]
B.source: Patanjali, Yoga Sutras I.14, I.21-22, tr. Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda vol. 1 (Wikisource).

B.line: Grandma Moses began painting in earnest in her late 70s. Her first solo show came at 80.
B.credit: Grandma Moses, painter · Smithsonian American Art Museum
B.exact: Moses began painting in earnest in her late 70s and was 80 when gallerist Otto Kallir introduced her to the American public with her first solo exhibition in 1940. [Wikipedia: she 'began painting in earnest at the age of 78'; the show 'What a Farm Wife Painted' opened at Galerie St. Etienne, New York, October 1940.]
B.source: Smithsonian American Art Museum, exhibition page 'Grandma Moses: A Good Day's Work'; English Wikipedia, 'Grandma Moses' (born 7 September 1860). Two sources agree.

B.line: The slower you ride, the farther you will get.
B.credit: Russian proverb · collected by Vladimir Dal (1862)
B.exact: Тише едешь - дальше будешь. [Literally: the quieter (slower) you ride, the farther you'll get.]
B.source: V. I. Dal, Пословицы русского народа (1862), section 'Путь, Дорога'. Checked on Russian Wikisource. English is our own translation.

B.line: You can't connect the dots looking forward. You can only connect them looking backwards.
B.exact: Again, you can't connect the dots looking forward. You can only connect them looking backwards. So you have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future. You have to trust in something, your gut, destiny, life, karma, whatever, because believing that the dots will connect down the road will give you the confidence to follow your heart even when it leads you off the well-worn path and that will make all the difference.
B.source: Steve Jobs, Commencement address, Stanford University, 12 June 2005. Wording as spoken, from NPR's transcript of the audio.

B.line: A vessel great, it is the slowest made.
B.credit: Laozi, Dao De Jing 41 · tr. James Legge
B.exact: Who progress in it makes, seems drawing back; ... A vessel great, it is the slowest made; [Chinese: 大器晚成]
B.source: Dao De Jing, ch. 41, tr. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism (Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891). Checked in the Standard Ebooks edition of Legge.

C.line: Life springs from sorrow and calamity, and death from ease and pleasure.
C.exact: Thus, when Heaven is about to confer a great office on any man, it first exercises his mind with suffering, and his sinews and bones with toil. It exposes his body to hunger, and subjects him to extreme poverty. It confounds his undertakings. By all these methods it stimulates his mind, hardens his nature, and supplies his incompetencies. ... From these things we see how life springs from sorrow and calamity, and death from ease and pleasure. [Chinese: 故天將降大任於是人也，必先苦其心志，勞其筋骨，餓其體膚，空乏其身，行拂亂其所為，所以動心忍性，曾益其所不能。……然後知生於憂患而死於安樂也。]
C.source: Mencius, Book VI (Gaozi) Part II, ch. 15 (6B.15), tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 2. Checked against the Wikisource transcription.

C.line: Ice crushed their ship. Six men sailed a small boat about 1,300 km for help. All 28 came home.
C.exact: After their ship Endurance was crushed in the ice, the party's 28 men reached Elephant Island. On 24 April 1916 Shackleton and five companions left in the small boat James Caird and sailed about 1,300 km to South Georgia, landing on 10 May. The 22 men left on Elephant Island were reached by the Yelcho on 30 August 1916, and 'within an hour they were all aboard'. Wikipedia: 'the entire Endurance crew returned home, without loss of life.'
C.source: Wikipedia, 'Voyage of the James Caird'; RSGS, Jo Woolf, 'Shackleton and the men on Elephant Island' (https://www.rsgs.org/shackleton-and-the-men-on-elephant-island-a-brotherhood-of-the-sea). Two sources agree. True for the Endurance party only, not the Ross Sea party.

C.line: Heat and cold, sorrows and joys... Bear with it... As the wise bear.
C.exact: Bringing thee heat and cold, sorrows and joys, / 'Tis brief and mutable! Bear with it ... / As the wise bear. The soul which is not moved, / The soul that with a strong and constant calm / Takes sorrow and takes joy indifferently, / Lives in the life undying! [Sanskrit 2.14: mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ / āgamāpāyino 'nityās tāṁs titikṣasva bhārata]
C.source: Bhagavad Gita, ch. 2, verses 14-15, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885), Project Gutenberg #2388.

C.line: Character cannot be developed in ease and quiet. Only through experiences of trial and suffering can the soul be strengthened.
C.credit: Helen Keller · Helen Keller's Journal (1938), p. 60
C.exact: No doubt the reason is that character cannot be developed in ease and quiet. Only through experiences of trial and suffering can the soul be strengthened, vision cleared, ambition inspired and success achieved.
C.source: Helen Keller's Journal: 1936-1937 (Doubleday, Doran & Co., 1938), p. 60. Checked in the archive.org scan. Note: the book says 'experiences' (plural) with no comma before 'and success achieved'.

C.line: Without work, you can't even pull a little fish out of a pond.
C.credit: Russian proverb · recorded by Vladimir Dal
C.exact: Чтобы рыбку съесть, надо в воду лезть. Без труда не вынешь и рыбку из пруда. [Literally: To eat a fish you must go into the water. Without labour you can't even take a little fish out of a pond.]
C.source: V. I. Dal, Толковый словарь живого великорусского языка, 2nd ed., entry «Рыба». Checked on Russian Wikisource. English is our own translation. If the modern «вытащишь» is used, credit only 'Russian proverb'.

C.line: A sword's sharp edge comes from grinding. The plum blossom's scent comes from bitter cold.
C.credit: Chinese saying · 宝剑锋从磨砺出，梅花香自苦寒来
C.exact: 宝剑锋从磨砺出，梅花香自苦寒来
C.source: Traditional Chinese couplet (author unknown), widely taught in Chinese schools

C.line: Fire tests gold, misfortune brave men.
C.credit: Seneca, On Providence 5.10 · tr. John W. Basore
C.exact: Fire tests gold, misfortune brave men. [Latin: Ignis aurum probat, miseria fortes viros.]
C.source: Seneca, De Providentia (On Providence) 5.10, tr. John W. Basore, Moral Essays vol. I (Loeb Classical Library, 1928). Checked in the stoics.com transcription of Basore.

C.line: What is needed is constant work, day and night, constant reading, study, will.
C.credit: Anton Chekhov, letter to his brother, 1886 · tr. Constance Garnett
C.exact: What is needed is constant work, day and night, constant reading, study, will.... Every hour is precious for it....
C.source: Anton Chekhov, letter to his brother Nikolay, Moscow, 1886, tr. Constance Garnett, Letters of Anton Chekhov to His Family and Friends (1920), Project Gutenberg #6408. Russian wording not yet checked against the Academy edition.

C.line: Tenzing Norgay went to Everest six times. On the seventh, in 1953, he and Hillary reached the top.
C.exact: Wikipedia: he 'had previously been to Everest six times'. On 29 May 1953 he and Edmund Hillary reached the summit at 11:30 a.m. Himalayan Journal: 'the seeds sown... bore fruit 18 years later'. Tenzing, Tiger of the Snows (1955): 'Seven times I have tried, I have come back and tried again; not with pride and force, ... but with love, as a child climbs onto the lap of its mother. Now at last I have been granted success, and I give thanks.'
C.source: Wikipedia, 'Tenzing Norgay'; Himalayan Club, Himalayan Journal vol. 43, 'In Memoriam' (https://www.himalayanclub.org/hj/43/22/in-memoriam-33/); Tenzing Norgay with James Ramsey Ullman, Tiger of the Snows (G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1955), ch. 1. Two sources agree on the years.

C.credit: Japanese proverb · 艱難汝を玉にす
C.exact: 艱難汝を玉にす (kannan nanji o tama ni su). Digital Daijisen: 人間は苦労・困難を乗り越えることによってりっぱな人物になる。
C.source: Digital Daijisen (Shogakukan) and Seisen-ban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, on Kotobank. A Meiji-era rendering of the Western proverb 'Adversity makes a man wise', first attested 1874; not ancient, not Chinese.
